solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Duck (present tense)

blocks.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A grammar note, as if telling you the verb duck is shown in the present tense.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make it look like a dictionary label, but they hold the wordplay. A duck in cricket is a score of zero; nowt is Northern English for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman's duck means a score of nothing, and northern dialect says nowt for nothing.

clue.text: A little resistance put up in farmhouse

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the next word of the clue
in a down clue, putting something up means writing it bottom to top

explanation.surface: A farmhouse family offers some mild opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance, so one ohm is a little of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ohm is the SI unit of electrical resistance, so a single one is a small amount.

clue.text: Set up modern sort of TV in public transport

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting something up raises it so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: a smart TV connects to the internet

explanation.surface: Installing the latest internet television on buses and trains.
explanation.definitionFit: Trams are streetcars running on rails in city streets, a form of public transport.

clue.text: Picked up wretched mess around musical instrument

indicators.note: picked up as in heard, so the next word counts by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: base means low and wretched; the musical word is said the same
to fiddle is to fidget or tinker

explanation.surface: Someone hears about a miserable bit of tinkering with an instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The double bass is often called the bass fiddle, the largest bowed string instrument in an orchestra.

clue.text: A jolly boring processed Brie getting more out to lunch

indicators.note: processed cheese is broken down and reformed, so the cheese's letters are rearranged
boring into something means going inside it

blocks.note: a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine

explanation.surface: A dull, mass-produced cheese makes a diner go dotty.
explanation.walkthrough: Jolly looks like an adjective but is a noun here: sailors' slang for a Royal Marine. Barmy is British for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is British slang for crazy, and someone out to lunch is mad, so more out to lunch is barmier.

clue.text: Cuts in NHS may be bound up with this

definitions.text: Cuts in NHS may be bound up with this

blocks.note: surface reading: budget reductions in Britain's National Health Service

blocks.clueFragment: may be bound up with this
blocks.note: setter's reading: wounds treated in hospital get covered with an adhesive dressing, which is also a phrase for a stopgap fix

explanation.walkthrough: The NHS is Britain's state health service. Cuts read as spending cuts, but they are wounds; the answer also means a quick fix that hides a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: This adhesive dressing covers small cuts, and figuratively names a temporary fix that does not cure the problem.

clue.text: The same treatment for all in moderately good parties

blocks.note: fair means middling, neither good nor bad

explanation.surface: Equal treatment for all guests at some passable parties.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair dos is British slang for even-handed treatment, giving everyone an equal share or fair deal.

clue.text: Chinese hybrid in empty desert bursting open

indicators.note: a hybrid is a mixed creation, so the nationality's letters are mixed
emptying a word leaves only its outside letters
something placed in another sits inside it

explanation.surface: A Chinese crossbred plant in a barren desert is splitting apart.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany a dehiscent pod or fruit splits open naturally when ripe to release its seeds.

clue.text: Holiday book about computers etc? I can cope with that

explanation.surface: Someone offers to handle a holiday read on computing.
explanation.walkthrough: A tome about IT is an IT tome, so the second piece is read after its subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a speaker volunteering to take a task on themselves, a promise of handling it.

clue.text: Current politician’s broadcast causing damage

blocks.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current
to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: A sitting politician's party broadcast does harm to their cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Politician's' reads as possessive, but the 's is just MP followed by the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair something is to weaken or harm it, so the verb is a synonym of damage.

clue.text: I’m European and I’m keeping quiet in a Middle Eastern country

definitions.note: the answer is the noun naming the speaker

indicators.note: something keeping a thing holds it inside, so the hush goes within the self-reference
placed in the country name, so the country's letters surround the rest

blocks.note: the sound for asking for silence

explanation.surface: A traveller in Iran says where they come from and that they are keeping their head down.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue has two I'm: the first belongs to the definition, the speaker introducing himself; the second is wordplay. Two containers nest here, one inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A man from Ireland is a European, so he could introduce himself with these words.

clue.text: Rod’s an idiot

blocks.note: first meaning: the measuring rod for a car's oil level
second meaning: slang for a fool

explanation.surface: A rude remark that a man named Rod is a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod looks like a man's name; it is the engine gauge.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the engine gauge used to check oil and, informally, a stupid person.

clue.text: For this embarrassing situation Grannie flat’s preposterous!

definitions.note: the answer is a Latin phrase meaning caught in the act

indicators.note: a preposterous thing is absurdly topsy-turvy, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written; a granny flat is an annexe for an elderly relative

explanation.surface: Someone is caught in an awkward moment in the annexe where Gran lives.
explanation.walkthrough: A granny flat is a self-contained annexe for an older relative; being caught there by Gran would be awkward indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being caught in flagrante, Latin for in the blazing act, means discovered doing wrong, usually sexually, which is embarrassing.

clue.text: Frustrated parent grabs female

indicators.note: whatever grabs something holds it, so the father figure wraps round the woman

explanation.surface: An exasperated father snatches hold of a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopes that are dashed are thwarted or ruined, so the past participle matches frustrated.

clue.text: More than one issue coming from temporarily unavailable vaults

blocks.note: a dish that is off the menu cannot be had today
to vault is to leap or spring

explanation.surface: Several matters arise from strongrooms that cannot be opened for now.
explanation.walkthrough: Vaults reads as a noun, strongrooms, but works as a verb, leaps. Issue means children in law.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a formal word for children, so a plural of the word for descendants means several issues.

clue.text: Time for entering board game over in tourist town

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end
letters entering go inside the other piece

blocks.note: darts is played by throwing at a board

explanation.surface: Time to play a board game while on holiday somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board game' suggests chess; it is the pub game played at a dartboard. Stratford-upon-Avon is Shakespeare's birthplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Stratford-upon-Avon, birthplace of Shakespeare, draws huge numbers of visitors, so it is a tourist town.

clue.text: Cockney makes hot food

indicators.note: a Cockney accent famously drops the aitch at the start of words

blocks.note: to heat is to make hot

explanation.surface: A Londoner's café warms up a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class East London accent, which leaves off the H. Eats is slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal speech uses the plural noun for snacks or a meal, as in a sign promising good eats.

clue.text: Standard boxes right for salmon

indicators.note: a box holds things, so the norm encloses the extra letter

blocks.note: par is the expected or normal level

explanation.surface: A boxing referee sets the usual rules for a fighter called Salmon.
explanation.definitionFit: A parr is a young salmon in its early freshwater stage, so it is an example of the fish.

clue.text: Without a job in large show

blocks.note: ex means without, as in shares sold ex dividend
a post or position is a job

explanation.surface: Someone unemployed in a big trade fair.
explanation.definitionFit: An exposition is a large public exhibition, such as a world fair, so it is a big show.

clue.text: Brave fellow’s gone without lugs

indicators.note: when something is gone it has been removed, so the man's abbreviation leaves

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A courageous man has lost his ears.
explanation.walkthrough: Lugs is British slang for ears.
explanation.definitionFit: Lugs is informal for ears, so something without lugs is earless, having no ears.

clue.text: Very legitimate request

blocks.note: so means very, as in so good

explanation.surface: A perfectly lawful application.
explanation.walkthrough: Request reads as a noun but is the verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To solicit is to ask for or seek something, making it a verb synonym of request.

clue.text: By the sound of it, comparatively large kitchen instrument

indicators.note: the phrase asks us to judge the next words by how they are spoken

explanation.surface: Something in the kitchen sounds rather bigger than you'd expect.
explanation.definitionFit: A grater is the kitchen tool with sharp holes used to shred cheese or vegetables.

clue.text: One US state, say, in a state!

explanation.surface: Naming a single American state, then exclaiming about being in a state.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'state' tempts you to read both alike; the first is Florida, the second means nervous agitation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone aflutter is nervously excited, and being in a state means being agitated or flustered.

clue.text: Unusual spurt coming from paint additive

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters are out of their usual order

explanation.surface: An odd squirt comes from something mixed into the paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Turps, short for turpentine, is a solvent used to thin oil paint and clean brushes.

clue.text: It’s fresh down by the Hampshire coast

blocks.note: being down by somewhere is being in it
the Solent is the strait between Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: A seaside report: the weather is brisk down on the south coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Fresh sounds like a breeze, but it means cheeky. Hampshire is a county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fresh with someone means being cheeky or impudent, a sense shared with the rude adjective.

clue.text: Stiff private secretary in central part

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is held inside it

blocks.note: the core is the heart of something

explanation.surface: A rigid secretary working at the heart of the office.
explanation.walkthrough: Stiff looks like an adjective but is slang for a dead body.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff is slang for a dead body, and a corpse is a dead body.

clue.text: The main part of anaesthetics taken up

indicators.note: only a portion of the long word is used
in a down clue, taking something up lifts it so it reads bottom to top

explanation.surface: The chief portion of the anaesthetic has been administered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' reads as 'the chief', but the main is an old poetic name for the open ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is a literary term for the open ocean, as in the Spanish Main.

clue.text: Jack Dee touring Europe, first in Paris tries improvised witty display

indicators.note: a touring party goes round a place, so the continent's letters go round the river's
the opening letter of the French capital's name is taken
something improvised is made up on the spot, so the letters are rearranged freely

blocks.note: J is jack in a pack of cards
dee is the spelt name of the letter D

explanation.surface: Comedian Jack Dee, on a European tour, tries out off-the-cuff material in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Dee is a British stand-up comic; his name splits into a playing card and the spelt-out name of a letter. Only the card stays outside the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeu d'esprit, French for a game of wit, is a light clever piece of writing or remark.

clue.text: Heartless person from Belgrade could be the guy at Number 10

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle letters are taken out

blocks.note: Belgrade is the capital of Serbia

explanation.surface: A cold-hearted Balkan figure might be the man living at Downing Street.
explanation.walkthrough: Number 10 looks like Downing Street, the British prime minister's home, but points to 10 across, IRISHMAN: Sean is an Irish name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sean is a typical Irish first name, so a man called this could be the Irishman of that entry.
